MoreSpace/Industries/Healthcare/Clinics & day-care centres

Fill the diary, prepare patients and keep recurring sessions on schedule

Clinics and day-care centers depend on punctual diaries: consultations, minor procedures and repeating dialysis, chemotherapy or physiotherapy sessions. We automate booking, preparation instructions, session schedules, day-care insurance paperwork and next-day check-ins, while the doctor's instructions stay the single source of truth.

What makes clinics & day-care centres different

  • A small front desk handles calls, walk-ins and billing at once, so WhatsApp messages wait and patients book elsewhere.

  • Patients arrive unprepared for procedures, for example without fasting or without previous reports, and the slot is lost.

  • Repeating dialysis, chemotherapy or physiotherapy sessions are tracked on paper, so a missed session may not be noticed until the next visit.

  • Insured day-care procedures need pre-authorization at short notice, often handled by the same person who answers the phone.

Where automation helps clinics & day-care centres

  • Booking that fits a doctor-led diary

    WhatsApp booking against the clinic EMR or calendar, with buffers the doctor sets around procedures and a waitlist that fills cancellations.

  • Preparation instructions patients act on

    Procedure-specific instructions written by the clinician, sent at the right time before the slot with a confirm button and a route to the nurse for questions.

  • Recurring session schedules

    Session series built from the treatment plan, chair and machine capacity checked, reminders sent, and missed sessions flagged to the nurse in charge the same day.

  • Day-care cashless paperwork

    Insurer-specific document checklists and secure upload links for patients, so the clinic submits a complete pre-authorization request before the procedure day.

  • Next-day check-ins

    Structured check-ins after day surgery, with any reported concern sent to the treating doctor's team instead of an automated reply.

  • Safe enquiry handling

    Fees, timings and directions answered from approved content; symptom messages handed to the clinic nurse, with an emergency instruction where needed.

Find and enquireStandard3–4 weeks

Safe enquiry routing for clinics and labs

Incoming WhatsApp and website messages are sorted by intent. Fees, timings, check-up packages, test preparation and directions are answered from approved content; symptoms, result questions and complaints go to the right staff member, and emergencies get an immediate instruction.

Clinics & day-care centres · Diagnostics & pathology labs

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Small teams cannot answer every message quickly, and generic chatbots either frustrate patients or, worse, attempt medical advice. Enquiries left unanswered often book elsewhere, while messages that describe symptoms need a qualified person, not a template.

Trigger

A patient sends a WhatsApp message to the clinic or lab number, or submits the website enquiry form.

How it runs

  1. Open a conversation linked to the CRM contact, creating it if new; replies inside the 24-hour service window need no template, and later follow-ups use approved templates only for patients who opted in.
  2. Screen each message first against the emergency word list agreed with the clinical lead; on a match, reply at once with the facility's emergency number and 112 and alert the duty staff.
  3. Classify the remaining text into intents such as fees, timings, check-up packages, test preparation, booking, report status, symptom or complaint, with a confidence score.
  4. Answer administrative intents only from the approved FAQ, rate card or test master, citing the entry used; low-confidence drafts are not sent.
  5. Hand symptom, medicine and result questions to the nurse or lab medical staff queue with a conversation summary, and tell the patient who will reply and when.
  6. Log intent, handoff reason and response times for a weekly review of wording and routing rules.

Human checkpoint

The clinic nurse or the lab's medical officer answers every symptom, medicine or result question; front-office staff take complaints and anything the model is unsure about. The clinical lead approves the emergency word list and the FAQ before go-live.

Book and prepareStandard4–6 weeks

WhatsApp appointment booking, reminders and rescheduling

Patients book consultations and health check-ups on WhatsApp against live HIS or EMR slots, receive approved reminders with preparation notes, and confirm, reschedule or cancel in one tap. Released slots go back to the diary and to the waitlist.

Multi-specialty hospitals · Clinics & day-care centres

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Phone booking lines queue at peak hours, patients forget appointments, and those who want to reschedule cannot get through. Slots go unused while others wait, and preparation instructions for check-ups and procedures are missed.

Trigger

An opted-in patient taps Book in WhatsApp or scans a booking QR code, or staff create a booking at the desk or by phone in the HIS.

How it runs

  1. Offer department, doctor, date and slot in a WhatsApp Flow, reading availability from the HIS or EMR scheduling API, or from a synced slot table where the system has no API.
  2. Write the booking back to the HIS, or queue it for front-office entry where there is no API, and confirm with preparation notes written by the department, such as fasting before a check-up.
  3. Send reminder templates at intervals the hospital sets, each with confirm, reschedule and cancel buttons.
  4. On reschedule or cancel, release the slot in the HIS and offer it to waitlisted patients in order of request.
  5. When a consultant's clinic is delayed or canceled, notify booked patients with an approved template once the OPD coordinator approves the message.
  6. Report bookings, confirmations, reschedules and no-shows by department and doctor.

Human checkpoint

Front-office staff handle anything outside the booking rules, such as priority appointments or patients who reply with symptoms, which go to the duty nurse. The OPD coordinator approves every delay or cancellation message before it is sent.

Arrive and registerStandard4–5 weeks

OPD pre-registration, ABHA Scan and Share and token updates

Patients pre-register before they arrive, can use ABHA Scan and Share where the facility participates, and receive their token and queue position on WhatsApp, so they can wait outside a crowded hall and return when called.

Multi-specialty hospitals · Clinics & day-care centres

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Morning OPD crowds form at registration and outside consulting rooms. Patients cannot tell how long they will wait, staff repeat the same answers, and a consultant held up in surgery means a full hall with no information.

Trigger

A booked patient is due today, or a patient registers at the desk, scans the facility's QR code or completes ABHA Scan and Share.

How it runs

  1. Send a pre-registration link in an approved template the evening before, so demographic details reach the HIS ahead of arrival.
  2. Where the HIS is ABDM-integrated, offer ABHA Scan and Share at the entrance as an optional route to registration and a token.
  3. On token issue, send the token number and a live position link that reads queue status from the HIS or token display system.
  4. Send a call-ahead message when the patient is a set number of places away, and a final call when the doctor is ready.
  5. If a consultant is delayed, send waiting patients a delay notice approved by the OPD coordinator, with the option to rebook.
  6. Flag the desk when a patient misses the final call, instead of skipping them automatically.

Human checkpoint

The OPD coordinator approves delay notices and decides on out-of-turn priority for elderly, pregnant or visibly unwell patients. Triage nurses, not the system, decide clinical priority.

Treatment and admissionStarter2–4 weeks

Recurring session scheduling for dialysis, chemo and physiotherapy

Treatment plans with repeating sessions become scheduled series with chair or machine capacity checked, reminders sent before each session, and missed sessions flagged to the nurse in charge the same day.

Clinics & day-care centres

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Day-care units manage repeating sessions in paper diaries or spreadsheets. Capacity clashes surface on the day, reminders depend on staff calling patients, and a missed dialysis or chemotherapy session may go unnoticed until the next visit.

Trigger

The treating doctor records a session plan, with frequency and duration, in the EMR or the unit's scheduling sheet.

How it runs

  1. Create the session series from the plan and check chair, machine and staff capacity for each date.
  2. Propose alternatives for clashes to the unit coordinator instead of moving sessions automatically.
  3. Send a reminder template before each session with any preparation notes the unit has written, plus confirm and cannot-attend buttons.
  4. When a patient cannot attend or does not arrive, alert the nurse in charge the same day with the patient's contact details.
  5. Update the series when the doctor changes the plan, and send the patient the revised schedule.

Human checkpoint

The unit coordinator approves schedule changes. The nurse in charge follows up every missed session and escalates to the treating doctor, who alone decides any change to the treatment plan.

Tools

Treatment and admissionAdvanced6–8 weeks

Cashless pre-authorization document tracker

Each insured admission or day-care procedure gets a live checklist of the documents its insurer or TPA needs, secure upload links for the family, timers on insurer queries and an alert when discharge authorization is waiting.

Multi-specialty hospitals · Clinics & day-care centres

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Pre-authorization requests stall on a missing ID, policy card or investigation report, and insurer queries sit in inboxes. IRDAI's 2024 health insurance master circular expects insurers to decide cashless authorization requests within one hour and final discharge authorization within three hours of the hospital's request, so incomplete files are the delay a hospital can fix.

Trigger

An admission or day-care procedure is marked cashless in the HIS, or the TPA desk opens a new pre-authorization case.

How it runs

  1. Create the case with the insurer or TPA's document checklist and a request for the treating doctor's estimate and clinical notes.
  2. Send the patient or family an approved template with a secure upload link for missing ID and policy documents.
  3. Use a model to read uploaded documents and pre-fill policy number, insured name and dates for the TPA executive to verify.
  4. Track submission and insurer queries from NHCX status where the hospital is connected, or as the TPA executive logs them from portals and email, with timers and reminders to the TPA desk and treating doctor.
  5. At discharge, alert billing and the TPA desk when final authorization is pending beyond the agreed internal window.
  6. Report cycle times by insurer, department and query type for the monthly review.

Human checkpoint

The TPA desk executive checks every extracted field and submits the request; the treating doctor writes and signs the clinical justification and answers medical queries. No document goes to an insurer automatically.

  • Insurer and TPA portals
  • National Health Claims Exchange (NHCX) where connected

Data & consent

Upload links expire, and masked Aadhaar copies are requested where the insurer accepts them. Extraction runs under enterprise model terms with no training use, and retention follows the hospital's insurance record policy.

  • Cycle-time dashboard by insurer and department

  • Discharge authorization wait
  • Insurer queries open beyond the agreed window

Discharge and continuing careStandard4–6 weeks

Discharge summary sharing and post-discharge follow-up

When the consultant signs the discharge summary, the patient receives a secure link, follow-up reminders and structured check-ins on the days the care team chose. Any reported concern goes to a care coordinator nurse, never to an automated reply.

Multi-specialty hospitals · Clinics & day-care centres

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Patients leave with paper summaries and verbal instructions, follow-up visits are missed, and early warning signs are reported late or at another facility. Care teams have no simple way to check in with every discharged patient.

Trigger

The treating consultant signs the discharge summary in the HIS or EMR.

How it runs

  1. Send an approved template with a secure, expiring link to the signed discharge summary to the patient or a family member the patient names, alongside the printed copy.
  2. Schedule the follow-up appointment reminder and the check-in days the care team recorded in the discharge plan.
  3. Ask check-in questions written by the clinical team, such as whether the patient has a concern to discuss, with yes and no buttons.
  4. Route any yes, free-text concern or missed check-in to the care coordinator nurse's queue with a short summary of the conversation.
  5. State in every message how to reach emergency care, and answer emergency words with the hospital's emergency number and 112.
  6. Book the follow-up visit in the HIS and report check-in completion by department.

Human checkpoint

A care coordinator nurse reviews every flagged reply and calls the patient, and the treating doctor decides any change to medicines or care. AI only summarizes free-text replies for the nurse and never advises the patient.

Tools

  • Follow-up appointment scheduling
